sit: You meet your friend Marcus in the forum. Greet him.
explain: _Salvē_ is the standard greeting, literally 'be well'. When you speak to someone by name, the name takes the vocative: for -us nouns the ending becomes -e, so _Mārcus_ → _Mārce_.
distractors: _salvēte_ greets several people. To one person, say _salvē_.

sit: You are leaving. Say goodbye to Marcus.
explain: _Valē_ is the command form of _valeō_ ('be well'), used when parting. To several people: _valēte_.
distractors: _valēte_ is addressed to several people. To one person, say _valē_.

sit: Ask your friend how he is.
en: How are you? (Literally: “What are you doing?”)
explain: Romans asked _Quid agis?_ ('What are you doing?') much as we say 'How are you?'. You can also ask _Valēsne?_ ('Are you well?'), where -ne turns the sentence into a question.
distractors: _agō_ is the 'I' form: 'What am I doing?'.
_ubi_ = where: 'Where are you doing?' doesn't work as a greeting.

sit: Tell your friend that you are well.
explain: _valeō_ means 'I am well, I am in good health'. Roman letters often began with a wish that you were well, using the same verb.
distractors: _valēs_ is 'you are well'. To talk about yourself, use _valeō_.

sit: Ask your friend whether he is tired.
explain: Add -ne to the first word to ask a yes/no question: _Fessusne es?_ or _Esne fessus?_. Without it, _Fessus es_ is a statement: 'You are tired.'
distractors: After _es_ the adjective stays nominative: _fessus_, not _fessum_.
Without -ne this is a statement: 'You are tired.'

sit: Someone has handed you a cup of water. Thank him.
en: Thank you. (Literally: “I give thanks to you.”)
explain: Romans said 'I give thanks to you': _grātiās tibi agō_. The person you thank is in the dative (_tibi_). You can also just say _Grātiās!_.
distractors: 'To you' needs the dative _tibi_, not the nominative _tū_.
_agis_ is the 'you' form, so this says 'you give thanks to you'.

explain: _quaesō_ literally means 'I ask'. What you ask for is its object, so it goes in the accusative: _aquam_.
distractors: The thing asked for is an object: _aquam_, not _aqua_.

sit: Someone is speaking too fast. Say that you don't understand.
explain: _intellegō_ means 'I understand'. Put _nōn_ in front to negate it.

sit: Tell someone that your name is Marcus.
tag: mihi nōmen est = my name is
explain: Latin says 'to me the name is Marcus' (_mihi nōmen est_). The name stays in the nominative. _Nōmen meum est_ ('my name is') is also fine.
distractors: The name stays nominative (_Mārcus_). The vocative is only for calling someone.
_nōmina sunt_ is plural: 'names'. You have one name.

sit: Ask a stranger what his name is.
tag: tibi nōmen est = your name is
explain: 'What is your name?' is 'What is the name to you?': _Quid tibi nōmen est?_ The same dative pattern as _mihi nōmen est_.

sit: Wish your friend a good night's sleep.
explain: The command form to one person is the verb stem: _dormī_ (from _dormīre_), _valē_ (from _valēre_). To several people add -te: _dormīte_.
distractors: _dormīte_ is a command to several people.
